# How We Cut Our Deploy Times by 70%

Shipping code used to be the worst part of our week. A full deploy took 40 minutes, and nobody wanted to merge on a Friday. Here is how we fixed it.

## The problem: cold builds

Every deploy started from scratch. Our CI pipeline recompiled everything, reinstalled every dependency, and rebuilt every container layer even when only one file had changed. Cache invalidation is famously one of the hard problems in computer science, and we were living it.

## How build caching actually works

A build cache stores the output of a build step keyed by a hash of its inputs. When the inputs do not change, the step is skipped and the cached output is reused. Content-addressable hashing means the key is derived from the content itself, so identical inputs always map to the same output. Docker layer caching works this way: each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer, and if the instruction and its context are unchanged, the layer is reused.

## What we changed

We reordered our Dockerfile so dependency installation happens before the application code is copied in, and we enabled our CI provider's remote cache backend.

> EDITOR: this section feels thin — either add the migration story or merge it into the previous section

Cache invalidation turned out to be the hard part, just like the old joke says. Getting cache hits was easy; knowing when *not* to trust the cache took us two incidents to learn.

## Results

Deploys now take 12 minutes. Merge queue throughput doubled, and Friday deploys are boring again, which is exactly what we want.
